question: The serious human rights violations in Ecuador in recent years include prison massacres with more than 500 victims, political persecution of opponents, attacks on the freedom of the press, and even a recent attack on a foreign embassy – a flagrant breach of the most basic rules of international law – resulting in the detention of a political asylum-seeker.

These events are in stark contrast to the objectives and values of the European Union ( Articles 2 and 3 of the Treaty on European Union and EU Charter of Fundamental Rights) and the conditions laid down in the EU-Ecuador trade agreement. The EU’s failure to react to these events undermines its commitment to its own objectives and values, and the effectiveness of its human rights clauses at international level.
In view of this: 1.

What specific measures is the Commission considering to ensure that Ecuador respects human rights and the national sovereignty of third countries, as laid down in international law and in the EU-Ecuador trade agreement?
Given the repeated violations of human rights and international law, is it considering activating the clause to temporarily suspend the trade agreement with Ecuador?
answer: The Trade Agreement between the EU, Ecuador, Colombia and Peru (1) establishes the respect of fundamental human rights as an essential element of the agreement. It foresees the holding of annual political dialogues, including an annual human rights dialogue (the 2024 edition took place on 23 April) to monitor compliance.

There is also a mechanism for Ecuadorian and EU civil society to raise concerns about the implementation of these commitments. The EU is carrying out a wide range of activities to support the government, independent institutions and civil society in their efforts to promote and protect human rights.

Our projects, including in the Amazon, have yielded very positive results, for many years, in areas such as gender and the fight against violence against women, the defence of the rights of indigenous peoples, children's rights and the rights of LGBTIQ communities.

The EU shares the assessment that Ecuador is going through a major social and security crisis and that ensuring the respect of human rights in the country remains a key priority. In this situation, it is even more important to maintain our dialogue and cooperation to support Ecuador’s democratic institutions and the promotion of human rights in Ecuador.

A suspension of the agreement is not currently under consideration and would be counterproductive in relation to those objectives. The violation of the premises of the Mexican Embassy in Ecuador, however, is a breach of international law (1961 Vienna Convention), and as such, not covered by the Trade Agreement.
The EU has clearly condemned this violation and continues to encourage its partners Mexico and Ecuador to solve their dispute through dialogue and to re-establish diplomatic relations.

Protocol of Accession of Ecuador to the Trade Agreement between the European Union and its Member States, of the one part, and Colombia and Peru, of the other part (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A22016A1224%2801%29); Trade Agreement between the European Union and its Member States, of the one part, and Colombia and Peru, of the other part (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/? uri=CELEX:22016A1224(01)&qid=1588594733909&from=EN).
